events.title: Oil and gas prices climb after Saudi Arabia closes east-west pipeline
events.summary: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil was up by around 3% to 108 US dollars (£80) on Monday morning. Your support helps us to tell the story From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Oil and gas prices have climbed higher after Saudi Arabia shut down a vital oil pipeline in response to a series of drone attacks. The world’s financial markets continue to be rocked by fighting in the Middle East that is causing further disruption to global supply of the key commodities, sending wholesale prices surging. UK natural gas prices were rising by around 5% to 209p per therm, which is a unit of heat energy – remaining at the highest level since December 2022. Over the weekend, Saudi Arabia was forced to shut down its east-west pipeline which has been a crucial route for oil exports since the Iran war disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea port at the pipeline’s end have more than doubled since the Iran war began, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). The Saudi foreign ministry blamed the attacks on several drones that came from Iraq and Iraq’s government pledged to investigate the attacks. Richard Hunter, head of markets at Interactive Investor, said: “This east-west pipeline, which links the Gulf to the Red Sea, had been moving several million barrels each day and inevitably causes additional supply constraints. “The development also suggests that the conflict is as far away from resolution as ever and the inflationary impacts of elevated oil products are starting to become keenly felt. “The CPI (Consumer Prices Index) report in the US, for example, showed that the major driver of the August inflation increase was gasoline, which increased by 3.9% over the month.” In the UK, wholesale fuel prices, particularly for diesel, have continued to surge on the back of the oil spikes and refining issues. Higher wholesale gas prices are also sparking fears about the impact to household energy costs over the winter months. The IEA said in a report last week that it was now predicting 2026 worldwide oil consumption to drop by 2.5 million barrels a day versus 2025 due to the supply disruption. events.title: UAE’s Al Tajir family put Scottish ‘ghost’ golf course up for sale
events.summary: An incomplete golf resort in Scotland, which is owned by a UAE family but has never opened to public, has been put on the market. Located near the world-famous Gleneagles course in Perthshire, gWest was intended to rival the quality of its historic neighbour. But few people have had the chance to play the course on a private gated resort set on an estate spanning more than 80 hectares. It was bought by the UAE’s Al Tajir family in 2007, with the tournament-standard course completed two years later. Mahdi Al Tajir, who in 1971 became the first UAE ambassador to the UK, was named the richest man in Scotland by The Sunday Times in 2013 and owns the Highland Spring water company which is based nearby. But a combination of the financial crisis, the Scottish independence debate and referendum, Brexit and Covid-19 meant the family felt that the time has never been quite right to take it to the next stage of investment. It means the 18th-century-inspired clubhouse remains a shell and plans for the rest of the resort – it has permission for up to 170 residential plots, a hotel and spa, leisure and entertainment facilities and staff accommodation – remain on hold. Offers for the resort are now being welcomed after the family decided to sell up, with property consultant Knight Frank instructed to find a buyer. Euan Kelly, partner at Knight Frank Edinburgh, said: “It is incredibly rare that an opportunity like gWest becomes available. We’re expecting a huge amount of interest from across the globe in what could be a once-in-a-lifetime asset: a substantial consented resort development site, with a golf course designed by a celebrated architect, in one of Scotland’s most prestigious leisure locations. “While the bold ambitions for the site have yet to fully come to fruition, a sale could see them take an important step forward and add another destination to Scotland’s, and Perthshire’s, strong tourist offering.” Celebrated course architect David McLay Kidd designed the championship-standard course and described the resort as “the best inland site I’ve ever seen for a golf course”. It sits in one of Scotland’s best-known golf and leisure corridors, to the west of Gleneagles between Perth and Stirling. The UK’s golf industry generated revenue of around £2.7 billion ($3.64 billion) in 2024/25, which is expected to rise to £3 billion for 2025/26. There are about 560 courses in Scotland – one fifth of the total in the UK. The gWest website says the course has been specifically designed to blend seamlessly with the landscape and enhance the far-reaching views of the surrounding hills and countryside. It says: “The views from the estate are extraordinary, with the Ochil Hills to the south, and to the west, across rolling hills and mountains, Ben Vorlich in Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park can be seen. “The estate extends 2.3 miles [3.7km] from east to west and is surrounded by natural land, the majority of which is also owned by the developer, ensuring the boundaries, access and views are protected. Two listed heritage sites of old forts are also located within the grounds of the resort and an ancient church lies just beyond.” Speaking in 2020, Mr Al Tajir’s son, Mohsin, said: “You want to invest. The next phase of gWest is another 50, 60, maybe £100 million. And, as a family, we're not willing to put that sort of money in if we don't know what the future is.” He said with concerns that taxes would go up, rather than becoming a tax haven if independence were to happen, “maybe it's not the place I need to put my money”. He said at the time he had played the course 20 or 30 times, and seemed to suggest he had struggled. He joked that while the course was built by a respected designer, “I’m a bad golfer”.

events.title: The real AI economy is being built by ordinary people
events.summary: Far from Silicon Valley pitch decks, workers across Asia and Africa are bypassing tech industry hype to quietly rewire their daily jobs — one prompt, workflow, and local problem at a time. Rest of World visited workers across Asia and Africa who are using AI to solve daily problems, make a living, and create new possibilities in their everyday lives. These profiles reveal how people choose to leverage artificial intelligence — what they are willing to delegate, which tasks they insist on handling themselves — and how access to cheap, powerful AI can expand the limits of what one person can accomplish. It’s proof the economic impact of AI is taking shape on a personal, local level as forces in Silicon Valley and China battle to command the global AI ecosystem. 🇳🇬 “I have invested my time but not my money” When Nureeyah Ogunmuyiwa decided to hire her first employee earlier this year, she faced an unexpected problem. The 24-year-old makeup artist, who caters to brides and bridal parties among others in Lagos, had never hired anyone before. With her business growing and Ogunmuyiwa stepping into content creation to promote her services, she knew she needed to hire help. But she didn’t know how to write a job description, what questions to ask in an interview, or what qualities to look for in candidates. Within minutes, the chatbot produced a complete hiring plan, including interview questions and a checklist to evaluate candidates. “ChatGPT was my hiring manager that made the process less of a hassle,” Ogunmuyiwa told Rest of World. “I told her that I needed someone reliable, and to let me know what to do and what to look out for. She gave me everything that helped me hire my amazing assistant.” That assistant now works alongside the AI one. Ogunmuyiwa first encountered ChatGPT a couple of years ago while working as a customer support officer at a Lagos logistics startup after graduating from university. She used it to rewrite emails so they sounded more empathetic to customers and professional to colleagues. When she left her job in 2024 to focus full time on the makeup business she had been building on the side since 2018, AI came with her. As a bootstrapped entrepreneur with a small budget, she said ChatGPT has become her “most reliable business partner.” Today, it plays multiple roles. It’s her social media manager, writing captions, suggesting suitable hashtags, and recommending content ideas that have helped attract new customers. It’s her sales coach, helping her refine client pitches so they sound “bold but not too salesy.” It also handles the math. Whenever she restocks beauty products, ChatGPT helps her calculate prices based on costs and profit margins, saving hours of manual calculations. “It saves me from punching each product in the calculator and then trying to do the mental work of arriving at a profitable price point,” Ogunmuyiwa said. Nearly half of Nigeria’s population now has internet access, with the majority connecting through smartphones. Ogunmuyiwa finds the convenience of access to AI bots on her phone very useful. ChatGPT has become one of her most visited apps, alongside WhatsApp Business and Instagram. She prompts it for the simplest tasks like setting reminders. She has organized her conversations with different labels: “Glam by Ree,” named after her business; “return to corporate” for her professional plans; and “my studio project” for creative planning. When Ogunmuyiwa recently moved her business from her dining room to a rented studio, she used AI to generate mood boards, which she shared with carpenters and electricians as they worked on the new space. As new AI tools appeared, she began experimenting beyond ChatGPT. After a friend recommended Anthropic’s Claude earlier this year, she reluctantly gave it a try, worried she’d have to teach another chatbot everything about her business from scratch. Eventually, she settled into using both but highly favors ChatGPT. Ogunmuyiwa recently moved her business into a rented studio and used AI to generate mood boards. Ogunmuyiwa shared AI-generated reference images with carpenters and electricians to design her new studio. Damilare Dosunmu Despite relying on AI throughout her business, Ogunmuyiwa hasn’t paid for either service because she feels the free version serves her purpose. “I have invested my time but not my money,” she said. “And I’m getting a great return.” She is open to a paid version in the future if needed, especially to generate images and mood boards. AI contributes roughly 5% to her business growth. “I can’t give all the credit to AI for giving my business structure because I made a personal decision,” Ogunmuyiwa said. “AI has really helped me to implement that structure in the best way possible. I spent less time on things I trust ChatGPT to handle.” That growing dependence sometimes worries her. At one point, she deliberately stopped using AI because she felt she was consulting it before making every decision.

events.title: Why the election could make Washington's looming next fiscal crisis harder
events.summary: The U.S. could breach the debt ceiling at some point in 2027. Fixing it could be hard. If Democrats capture one or both chambers of Congress in November's midterm election, it would open the door to a standoff as the party tries to extract policy wins from Republican President Donald Trump in exchange for averting a bumpy ride over the fiscal cliff. If Democrats win in November, Republican hopes to remedy the issue while they control Congress could also be in trouble, as some in the GOP are already disavowing raising the debt ceiling without accompanying deep spending cuts. Washington's next fiscal crisis looms right around the corner. Fixing it could be hard. Analysts project the U.S. will breach the $41.1 trillion debt ceiling at some point in 2027, requiring Congress to raise or suspend it before the Treasury Department runs out of "extraordinary measures" to avoid a catastrophic default. If Democrats capture one or both chambers of Congress in November's midterm election , it would open the door to a standoff as the party tries to extract policy wins from Republican President Donald Trump in exchange for averting a bumpy ride over the fiscal cliff. Trump last week also proposed a $5,000 dividend for every American if Republicans win the midterms — a move that could bring the U.S. to the debt ceiling faster. And while some Republicans have proposed raising the debt ceiling this year to preempt potential brinksmanship next year — possibly during the lame-duck legislative session immediately after the election — some in the GOP are already disavowing such a move without deep spending cuts as the national debt balloons past $40 trillion, a record high. "There are already discussions like if we lose the midterms, it would probably need to happen in the lame duck," said Rep. Eric Burlison , R-Mo. "Because I don't think that the president wants to have a pound of flesh extracted by the Democrats." Burlison has proposed a constitutional amendment to require the U.S. government balance its budget and has called for capping future federal borrowing. Burlison, however, also said that "a blanket raise is not going to get my vote." "If you're a fiscal conservative, we should be using every opportunity that we can to reduce the deficit anytime we have a vote to raise the debt ceiling," he said. Other conservative lawmakers agreed, citing recent rises in Treasury yields as a reason to cut spending and not approve blanket approvals of more borrowing. "Not without massive spending restraint and reforms," said Rep. Chip Roy , R-Texas, a member of the ultra-conservative House Freedom Caucus, when asked by CNBC if he would support raising the debt ceiling before the end of the year. "If we're going to sit down and do the debt ceiling or sit down and talk about anything tax-related, then we're going to have to be real about spending restraint, so we'll see," Roy said. Analysis: Hot inflation data sets up a Fed rate hike. What happens if Warsh wavers Hassett kept up to $5 million Coinbase stake as Trump reshaped crypto policy Trump's energy holdings have surged as the Iran war moved oil markets That leaves Republican leaders Speaker Mike Johnson , R-La., and Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., between a rock and a hard place. Johnson has a razor-thin margin in the House and can only afford three defections on a party-line vote. And votes from Democrats, who are likely to balk at any major cuts to spending programs frequently targeted by Republicans, would be required to lift debt ceiling legislation over the 60-vote filibuster threshold in the Senate. Democrats will also be hesitant to agree to raise the debt ceiling if they win the election in November, given that it represents one of their most crucial points of leverage over the White House. "I would like to see exactly what their proposal would be and compare it to what we can possibly do in the majority," said Rep. Suhas Subramanyam , D-Va. "If they're going to try to jam us in the lame duck, we are not going to go along with it." It wouldn't be the first time the debt ceiling has been used as leverage by a majority party in Congress when the opposite party controls the White House. In 2023, House Republicans led by then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy brought the country to the brink of default before striking a deal with then-President Joe Biden to cut spending in exchange for raising the debt ceiling. Republicans were able to secure multiple policy wins during that episode, despite only controlling one chamber of Congress. Even with the potential leverage, however, some Democrats are taking a cautionary tone on the debt ceiling. Past debt ceiling standoffs, though not ending in default, have harmed the U.S.' credit standing. Fitch downgraded the U.S. from AAA to AA+ after the last standoff, saying "repeated debt-limit political standoffs and last-minute resolutions have eroded confidence in fiscal management." Rep.

Tom, a lot of this discussion this week is being spurred on by an op-ed you wrote this week about some warnings issued by a former Anthropic researcher who is making some pretty dire warnings that a lot of his colleagues seem to agree with. So what exactly was he getting at in this warning he issued? Everyone's saying that's really dangerous and could kill us all. If you installed this stuff in a nuclear missile silo and asked it to manage it for us, there's a good chance it could kill you all. So a lot of companies are already ahead of the game here. Brandon (03:11) Sure. We've written countless stories about deleted production databases, ruined systems, wiped drives, and all kinds of stuff. I feel like it's been going on for years now and the AI is only more advanced, so companies are probably even more hesitant. Tobias Mann (03:26) It's also not like there isn't a good template for building sandboxes that work. Tom (03:32) Yes. Brandon (03:33) Sure. Tobias Mann (03:33) If you look at every DOD or DOE supercomputer that is used to support our nuclear armament, those are all air-gapped systems. They could build proper air-gapped sandboxes for these things. They're choosing not to. Tom (03:56) Of all the things that are killing people right now, you'd have to go pretty far down the list to find AI actually killing people. There are some use cases starting to happen in Ukraine with drones where you get fully AI-powered target selection and things like that. Occasionally, a car with an AI vision system will hit someone. Brandon (04:41) Because again, this is all based on emergent behavior that hasn't emerged yet. It's just ridiculous, let alone the environmental cost of these things. If these companies are actually so concerned, they should stop. If you find yourself working on something that you think is going to kill everyone, do something. Don't just sit there and wait for your stock options to vest. Brandon (05:13) What about those investors? That's the problem we have. It's all about making money right now. I mean we've got two companies at the forefront of this thing, the two whose employees are independently, quote unquote, complaining the most about the risk of this stuff. They're hoping to be appointed to some position in the market where their word is unassailable and everyone else has to ask them for permission to do things. events.title: Washington's AI paralysis: Let 'er rip vs. hit the brakes
events.summary: President Trump is as all-in on AI as a politician could be: all gas, no brakes, and zero interest in hand-wringing about dystopian risks or public disdain. Democrats are as conflicted on AI as a party could be: skeptical of the labs, spooked by their warnings, but split on whether to shut it all down. Why it matters: This staggering divide makes consensus on federal AI regulation almost unimaginable this year — and probably through early 2029, regardless of who wins control of Congress. Zoom in: Trump has governed as the AI president from Day 1 , applying the same doctrine to models and the data centers that power them — build faster, regulate less, beat China. Speaking in Ireland on Sunday, he dismissed new safety warnings as the work of "a lot of negative forces ... bringing up things that won't happen" — and reduced the stakes to one line: "Whoever wins AI wins." It's unclear which "negative forces" Trump has in mind: Calls to slow the race — or " pace the frontier " — are now coming from the leaders of America's premier AI labs, including Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google. Between the lines: Trump's accelerationist allies, including venture capitalists in Silicon Valley, see the safety alarms as a cynical ploy by the field's dominant players to lock in favorable regulations. David Sacks, Trump's former AI czar and a leading voice for the administration's hands-off approach, has a simple answer : Slow yourselves down. If OpenAI and Anthropic truly think the frontier is moving too fast, Sacks argues, they can decelerate on their own without using Washington to force competitors to do the same. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) echoed Sacks' argument that the labs don't need Congress to slow themselves down — and rejected calls for an emergency moratorium. Johnson said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that he'd recall the House and put AI regulation to a vote "if we had the solution," but warned Congress against rushing into rules it doesn't yet understand. His preferred first step is a summit: Johnson said Sunday he wants Trump, congressional leaders and the heads of the major AI labs in a room as soon as possible to hammer out a common approach to safety. The other side: Congressional Democrats are coalescing around urgency, but have no comparable doctrine on what to actually do. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says his caucus will meet Tuesday to debate what action to take, while former President Barack Obama is privately urging the party to make AI a top priority. The policy spectrum is vast — and doesn't neatly map onto what the labs themselves are asking for. On the progressive end, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) want to ban superintelligence outright, pause advanced AI development and threaten violators with up to 20 years in prison . Others are reaching for more conventional Washington fixes: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) wants a bipartisan AI select committee with subpoena power, while Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is demanding that OpenAI open its models to federal safety reviews. What to watch: The unprecedented push for restraint from inside the AI industry, colliding with deepening public unease, could scramble this political stalemate. Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers, a Trump ally running in a swing state, said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's new warning convinced him "we must slow down development" so government can catch up. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) is investigating AI's "existential risk," while Sens. John Thune (R-S.D.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) are pursuing a narrower plan requiring companies to test and report catastrophic risks. Reality check: Political pressure and lobbying could crack open the door to narrow bipartisan measures, though any meaningful regulation would still have to survive Trump's veto pen. The bottom line: Washington is deeply divided on whether AI is a national triumph to unleash or a national emergency to contain.

events.title: At least one dead, 25 missing after boat carrying migrants sinks off Greece
events.summary: At least 51 people rescued as search operation continues off the island of Gavnos near Crete. One person has died, 25 are missing and 51 people have been rescued after a boat carrying migrants sank off a Greek island near Crete, according to the country’s coastguard. “Fifty-one were picked up by two boats that were in the area,” a coastguard spokesman said on Monday. list 1 of 3 Italy suspends free movement with Spain: Is Schengen in crisis after Ceuta? list 2 of 3 Greece reopens Syrian and Afghan asylum cases, hoping for returns list 3 of 3 Eight bodies recovered in Libya, Greece as Mediterranean death toll rises He said survivors had reported that 77 people were on board when the boat went down near the island of Gavdos. Search and rescue efforts were ongoing, with four ships, boats, Frontex aircraft and a coastguard helicopter operating in the area, Greece’s public broadcaster ERT News reported. The 51 rescued people were due to be brought to Crete, “where the prescribed procedures will be followed”, ERT reported. After arriving in Crete, undocumented migrants generally face immediate arrest and temporary confinement before being transferred to closed detention camps on the Greek mainland. Under Greek law, individuals are subject to extended administrative detention, severe penalties and fast-track deportation. Strong winds blowing through the area have been hampering the search operation, ERT said. Crete and Gavdos, about 320km (200 miles) from the Libyan coast, have become the main point of entry for asylum seekers in Greece. In late August, Greece’s ANA news agency published figures from the Ministry of Migration and Asylum that indicated that migrant arrivals in the country fell from about 61,000 in the year to August 2025 to 42,000 in the following 12 months – a decline of about 31 percent. Greece’s conservative government in July suspended all asylum claims for migrants arriving by sea from North Africa for three months, a move it argued helped deter crossings. The ban passed in parliament amid a surge in asylum seekers reaching Crete and after talks with Libya’s Benghazi-based government to stem the flow were cancelled in July. The government remains at odds with regional authorities in Crete over a plan to build a permanent transit facility on the island. It is preparing draft legislation that would mandate imprisonment for people whose asylum claims are denied and require ankle monitors during a 30-day compliance period before deportation. Authorities in Europe have tightened their immigration rules over recent years as far-right, anti-immigrant political parties have won increasing support throughout the continent. Greece has been in discussions with Germany and several other European Union countries on setting up “return hubs” outside the bloc for processing migrants’ claims.

events.title: Abu Dhabi's Miral to invest Dh12bn over five years on more Yas Island hotels and attractions
events.summary: Miral , the company behind Yas Island in Abu Dhabi, has announced a Dh12 billion ($3.26 billion) investment over the next five years to expand its hospitality and theme park offerings. The amount will be allocated towards the expansion of a Warner Bros-themed hotel with 250 rooms, as well as a new lifestyle hotel at Yas Bay, Miral's group chief executive Mohamed Al Zaabi said at the Arabian Travel Market in Dubai on Monday. “We want to increase the room number today by almost 35 per cent in the coming five years,” he said. Among the new hotels, two will be based on themed IPs, based on increased demand for such units, he said, without disclosing details of the brands. The investment also encompasses the Harry Potter-themed expansion of its Warner Bros theme park, set to open in 2029. New rides in Ferrari World, Warner Bros and other new experiences will also be revealed as part of the expansion plans, Mr Al Zaabi said. The investment will be sourced mainly from Miral's earnings. “There will be a percentage that will be financed and we will try to use our resources to fund those projects,” he said. Disneyland Abu Dhabi Mr Al Zaabi also confirmed that progress on the new Disneyland Abu Dhabi theme park, which is not part of the Dh12 billion investment pipeline, is proceeding. “I'm very happy with the progress … we work hand in hand with Disney and we meet them literally every month,” he said. He did not reveal any dates for the opening of the theme park, which is also set to come up on Yas Island. Miral said its investment in new projects will support job creation and skills development in the tourism sector while enhancing Abu Dhabi's tourism experience. The investment signals a commitment to Abu Dhabi’s long-term tourism, Mohamed Al Mubarak, chairman of Miral, said in a statement. “Yas Island has become a global success story, demonstrating how world class experiences contribute to economic growth, enhance quality of life, and strengthen Abu Dhabi’s appeal to audiences from around the world.” Abu Dhabi’s Tourism Strategy 2030 plans to boost visitor numbers to 39.3 million, increase the sector's GDP contribution to Dh90 billion and create 178,000 new jobs within the tourism ecosystem. Mr Al Zaabi said: “We are not competing regionally, we are competing internationally. Tourists in India, China, any tourist market, the first thing they see [when researching destinations] is their mobile phone. [People have] worldwide access, so you are head to head with Paris, you are head to head with London, New York, Orlando.” The key is to stand out and having indoor theme parks makes the emirate a unique summertime destination, he added. Miral did not close any of its theme parks during the Iran conflict. Occupancy levels at the hotels on Yas Island were supported by staycation guests, he said. “Since June, we have seen a positive trend,” Mr Al Zaabi said. Along with the UAE market, they have been receiving visitors from the Gulf, India and Russia. “In general, I see a positive trend and we are very optimistic about the coming months as well,” he said. “I think next year will be a very good year for us.”

Theo Wargo/NBC/Getty Images Michael Polansky cofounded Outer Bio, a biotech company researching human skin. His fiancée, Lady Gaga, sits on the company's board of directors. Outer Bio is training AI models on data collected from skin samples. Michael Polansky is busy. In the last decade, he's cofounded a philanthropic nonprofit, launched an early-stage venture capital firm, helmed an asset management firm, got engaged to Lady Gaga , and somehow, had time to become a Grammy-nominated artist for co-writing seven songs on his fiancée's sixth studio album, "Mayhem." He and Lady Gaga also just welcomed their first child together. He's no stranger to the spotlight, but one of his most ambitious projects to date has remained largely unknown to the public. "We made the decision internally that we weren't going to talk about what we were doing until the data we generated was publication worthy," Polansky told Business Insider. That moment came late last month. "We are building the future of skin health," Lady Gaga, whose real name is Stefani Germanotta, wrote on X on August 21. "Welcome from Michael, Me and the entire team at Outer Bio." Meet @outerbio and YUNA. We are building the future of skin health. https://t.co/0PsbHPTIAX Welcome from Michael, Me and the entire team at Outer Bio. — Lady Gaga (@ladygaga) August 22, 2026 Founded in 2020, Outer Bio is a Massachusetts-based company that studies human skin to discover new bioactive ingredients, or compounds that can affect living tissue. Ideally, for Outer Bio, those ingredients could be used across a variety of industries, from pharmaceutical to beauty. Lady Gaga sits on the board of directors. "If you imagine products in Ulta or CVS, they have all sorts of active ingredients in them," Polansky said. "We would have proprietary active ingredients in products that were sold by other people." Outer Bio's research Studying human skin is tricky. Conducting tests on living people is highly regulated and an ethical minefield, while options like artificial skin and lab-grown organoids don't provide the same insights as actual skin. Plus, skin living outside the body can die quickly, making it difficult to conduct long-term studies. That's where Yuna, a research and development system Outer Bio developed in 2022, comes into play. It can keep living, full-thickness human skin observable for four weeks, the company says. The platform includes a 3D printed support structure that helps deliver nutrients to the skin tissue and remove waste. Yuna helps keep skin tissue alive and observable for up to four weeks. Outer Biosciences Yuna is just one cog in Outer Bio's machine, though. Outer Bio also collects donated living skin samples from a network of sources — hospitals, biobanks, medical research centers — that are typically left over from surgery or elective medical procedures. The team processes the skin tissue in-house, sometimes turning a single piece into dozens of samples. Then, the skin is prepped for experimentation and placed in custom-made well plates. Outer Bio says it is focused on several research areas, including wound healing, pigmentation, chronic inflammation, aging, and skin barrier function. Outer Bio collects donated skin samples for its research. Outer Biosciences "We will often remove samples throughout the month to collect data at different points in time," Polansky said. "Every single experiment has the freedom to be different depending on what the questions are and what the data is. Then that goes through our data generation process." The company uses AI models trained on the data it collects to predict which compounds could have bioactive or toxic effects on human skin. The skin is processed by its systems, and the results are fed back into the AI models to improve their predictive capabilities. Polansky said that data collection is Outer Bio's north star. "We're moving into an era where the amount of innovation that's needed in biology and life sciences is going too slowly," Polansky said. "I think that the only way that goes faster is that we have better data." Polansky said there's been progress in the biology and life sciences fields, but biological data collection for AI models is still growing. "We think of ourselves as a data company first and foremost," Polansky said. "We're not generative AI. We're predictive AI." Partnerships Although Outer Bio is focused on data, they've also secured partnerships with companies that can turn the bioactive ingredients they've discovered into real products. "As we discover chemicals or mechanisms that have immediate commercial or human relevance, it would be silly not to take advantage of that," Polansky said. Lady Gaga's cosmetics brand, Haus Labs, was an early partner with Outer Bio. Polansky also sits on the board of directors for Haus Labs. "The Haus Labs partnership is unique because Stefani and I are both involved with both companies," Polansky said. "It's super aligned, but we are working with other beauty companies that do totally different things with us than what Haus Labs does. Haus Labs' ambitions around innovation are very unique to them." Polansky said that, ultimately, Outer Bio can push forward the skin health industry and biological machine learning. "One of the things that I like about this company is that it truly is a scientific and technical problem that is very hard," he said. "No matter how long it took us to solve it, it would've been worth it because it opens up so many possibilities." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: He had a gig mowing lawns at 11. By 25, he had turned it into a multimillion-dollar landscaping business.
events.summary: Cody Kuebler, 25, started mowing his neighbors' lawns when he was 11. CLK Landscape Construction He began by cutting neighbors' grass for about $25 a lawn. A move at 14 meant rebuilding his customer base from scratch. He now oversees millions of dollars' worth of equipment — and works six days a week. Some kids mow lawns for pocket money and move on. Cody Kuebler kept at it, turning the childhood gig into a multimillion-dollar business. Now 25, Kuebler said he spent his summers growing up cutting his neighbors' grass for around $25 a job, first with an aging push mower, and later with one his father gave him for his 11th birthday. The gift involved "a little bit of horse-trading," he said: He'd have to cut his dad's lawn. Along the way, he hired friends so he could take on more customers and expand into snow removal during the winter months. Eventually, he earned enough to invest in riding lawn mowers with wagons attached. "I got a little taste of earning money and being my own boss," Kuebler told Business Insider. "That kind of stuck in my head." Business Insider's Young Geniuses series spotlights the next generation of founders, innovators, and thinkers trying to reshape industries and solve global challenges. See more stories from the series here , or reach out to editor Peter Gelling to share your story. Getting to where he is today, though, took grit and determination. Kuebler's parents divorced when he was 10, and a few years later, he moved from his childhood home in a small Iowa town to Des Moines after his father got a new job there. That meant having to start his fledgling business all over again. "It was frustrating because I had built a decent amount of customers that I lost over a decision I didn't make and couldn't change," Kuebler said. He pressed ahead, though as high school graduation approached, Kuebler wasn't sure his business could lead to a career. Since he is a car enthusiast and had already earned enough credits to graduate, he said he spent part of his senior year studying diesel mechanics at a local community college. He dropped out during the first semester, concluding he'd spent enough time in the classroom. Kuebler also considered working in sales. He got a job at a tire shop, but said his boss wasn't interested in pursuing ideas he had to grow the business. That experience clarified his own ambitions. "I always knew I wanted to do more in life," Kuebler said. "What that was, I didn't know at the time, but what I did know was how to cut grass." So Kuebler quit the tire shop to focus on his lawn-mowing and snow-removal venture, starting by setting it up as a limited liability company, or LLC, called CLK Landscape Construction. It was March 2020, a time that turned out to be ideal, as the pandemic was getting underway. Over the next two years, sales ballooned nearly ninefold to around $730,000. "What Covid actually did was keep people home, looking at their lawns," he said. "The landscaping market just boomed." Kuebeler directs employees at a construction site. CLK Landscape Construction Leveling up As Kuebler took on larger landscaping jobs, he needed heavier equipment. After a week of rain prevented him from using a skid loader he'd rented, he began visiting dealerships in hopes of acquiring one of his own. The machine Kuebler wanted cost about $80,000, and he needed a loan. Just 19 at the time, he said most of the salespeople he approached didn't take him seriously. One interrupted their conversation to answer a phone call and never returned to it. Eventually, Kuebler found a dealer willing to back him, and today his business has nine skid loaders and two mini skid loaders, plus 18 trucks, 12 trailers, 2 tractors, and a mini excavator. He said the equipment is worth about $2.5 million, and that some of it is owned, and some is leased. "You just got to keep pushing because a lot of people don't see the vision," he said of what it takes for young entrepreneurs to get ahead when others have doubts about their age or experience. In 2022, drawn to the complexity of builder-led projects, Kuebler began shifting from servicing homeowners to residential and commercial builders. The expansion brought a new set of challenges—and some expensive lessons. Kuebler said he underbid some jobs, missed deadlines, and lost customers. His company once had to redo a job when water failed to drain properly, while equipment breakdowns and projects that took longer than expected cut into profits. "Don't be scared to fail," Kuebler said, because despite those setbacks, his business reached $1.1 million in sales in 2023, $3.2 million in 2024, and $4.5 million last year. "We fail a lot." Tradeoffs Kuebler, right, with his father CLK Landscape Construction To be sure, Kuebeler's persistence has come at a steep cost to his free time. He said he typically works from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., six days a week, juggling everything from preparing quotes for prospective customers to reviewing jobs in progress and overseeing quality control. "The amount of work we do takes time to get done," he said. Despite the grueling schedule, Kuebler said he enjoys being his own boss and makes a comfortable living. He pays himself a $100,000 annual salary, plus an annual bonus that can increase his total compensation by 80% to 100%, depending on the company's net results. What's more, Kuebler's business has become a family affair: The father who gave him his first new mower now works for him as operations manager. "It was an easy hire," said Kuebler. "Obviously, he looks out for the company's best interest. He's blood-tied to it, and we get along great." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 2027 cars are rolling in slower than usual. That's good news for 2026 buyers.
events.summary: Fresh-faced 2027 cars are taking their time to reach dealerships. Here's what that means for buyers. Kevin Carter/Getty Images 2027's cars are arriving fashionably late: just 12.4% of new inventory is 2027. Several brands are just getting started with their 2027 model-year shipments. The slower switch could help patient shoppers score a deal on a 2026 model later this fall, analysts say. The auto industry is clinging to 2026. At the end of August, just 12.4% of new-vehicle inventory was 2027 model-year, according to CarGurus data shared with Business Insider. That's a sharp break from recent patterns: At the same point in each of the past three years, roughly one-quarter of new dealership inventory was for the next model year. Kevin Roberts, the director of economic and market intelligence for CarGurus, told Business Insider that the transition looks similar to the period from 2020 through 2022, when the industry was dealing with Covid-era assembly-line shutdowns and chip shortages . This year is different and less existential, he said, because "a lot of factors all came together to create something kind of unique this year." High-volume cars are driving the trend GM's best-selling vehicle, the Silverado, gets a fresh design for 2027. Chevrolet America's most popular cars are showing up late to the 2027 party. Erin Keating, Cox Automotive's executive analyst, told Business Insider that the trend is largely powered by big-name vehicles getting refreshed designs at different times. "In several cases, what looks like a slowdown at the brand level is really individual models rotating," she said. "It's important not to read this as uniform across a brand's whole lineup." GM is the cleanest example. The Detroit automaker has redesigned the Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra for 2027, with assembly of the new trucks expected to begin in October. The pickups are the company's best sellers, so a later handoff keeps an outsize number of 2026 models in the market. Other examples are more idiosyncratic, but still focused on best-sellers. Nissan's high-volume Rogue received a 2026.5 model year. Toyota's ever-popular RAV4 got its 2026 update in calendar 2025, making a quick switch to a 2027 version less likely. Honda is still sending fresh 2026 models to dealerships, too, Roberts said. The car company told Business Insider that some of its best-selling 2027 CR-V SUVs have reached dealerships, but model year changeover "is not fixed to a specific month, quarter, or time of year." "The 2027 model-year rollout is picking up speed but running behind last year's schedule," Keating said, adding that Kia, Cadillac, and BMW are already well into the model year switch. "It's an uneven transition, though." Deals to come? The tardy model-year switchover could bring lower prices. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Cars are expensive . The average transaction price for a new vehicle climbed back above $50,000 in August, according to Cox Automotive data. Keating said the later model-year transition could help "keep prices more stable," rather than pushing them down. Normally, freshly designed cars also come with higher prices. Patient shoppers may still find an opportunity, Roberts added. As 2027 inventory arrives in greater numbers, dealers will have more reason to move remaining 2026 models. "Eventually you'll start to see better deals for consumers on incentives," he said. "The timing might be a little bit more delayed this year." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Etihad expects 2026 break-even and strong demand despite Iran war
events.summary: Etihad Airways expects to break even this year due to strong demand despite the Iran war, reversing a forecast in June that it could post an annual loss. The Abu Dhabi airline is flying with planes 90 per cent full, generating positive cash flow and benefitting from a “booming” air cargo business, chief executive Antonoaldo Neves told The National on Monday at the Arabian Travel Market. The airline added 15 per cent capacity in July year-on-year, recorded a profit in August and held air fares at the same rate as last year despite an increase in jet fuel prices. "We are breaking even this year. We are not budgeting for a loss this year. We see demand very, very strong," he said. This comes after Etihad posted record annual profit after tax of Dh2.6 billion ($707.9 million) in 2025, up 47 per cent on 2024. In June, Mr Neves said the airline was unlikely to make a profit or may break even depending on the second half of the year. The prediction came as the Iran war disrupted regional air travel, leading to longer routes and higher jet fuel prices. Mr Neves said the airline was only one to two per cent behind its budget for the year, with growth of 15 per cent in Available Seat Kilometres (ASKs), a measure of its total passenger-carrying capacity, compared with the original target of 18 per cent. Etihad is "doubling the bet" as it continues to buy planes, hire talent and invest in new products, he said. The airline currently operates 320 flights a day, which it plans to increase by 25 per cent by the end of next year to about 400 flights, he added. Etihad had undergone years of restructuring before it returned to annual net profitability in 2022, ending a streak of losses that began in 2016. Asked whether the regional crisis would exert pressure on the airline's achievements, Mr Neves said: "This situation was a great test for Etihad ... we passed the test." He referred to the airline's ongoing investments in people and products, a strong balance sheet and continued cash generation this year. "We have the ability to absorb the crisis. If this was before 2019, we'd be going to cost-cutting mode," he said, referring to the airline's restructuring phase. "The model was tested, and the model response was the right one. We're confident about keeping investing. Things are going to improve and have been improving." Next wave of growth The next wave of growth next year will come from markets in China and Africa, with a focus on Latin America in 2028 or 2029, Mr Neves added. The airline has been adding an average of 20 destinations per year over the last couple of years in a burst of rapid growth, taking it to about 120 destinations currently. The lastest announcement is a flight to Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast from October 4. Etihad has a list of 10 priority countries in which it is pursuing airport slots or traffic rights, including to the island nation of Mauritius, South East Asia, Middle East and Europe, he said.

events.title: Yemen gov’t forces advance in Taiz as Houthis claim attack on Saudi Arabia
events.summary: Yemeni government forces have advanced in western Taiz after successfully repelling a Houthi offensive. Armed forces affiliated with Yemen’s internationally recognised government have retaken positions from the Houthis and are advancing in the southwestern Taiz province as clashes intensify. Reporting from Taiz on Monday, Al Jazeera Arabic’s Yasser Hassan said forces loyal to the Saudi Arabia-backed Yemeni government advanced in western Taiz on Sunday after successfully repelling a Houthi offensive. list 1 of 3 More than 2,000 Yemenis flee to Djibouti as fighting intensifies list 2 of 3 The Houthis’ escalation in Yemen could flop list 3 of 3 Fighting continues between Yemen gov’t forces, Houthis: What is the latest? “This comes with the support of air strikes targeting Houthi gatherings. The air force continues to bomb the Houthis. On the west coast in Mocha, Dhubab, and their surroundings,” Hassan said, citing a source in government forces. In a statement on Monday, the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), said they launched attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia using dozens of ballistic missiles and drones. The group said the attacks targeted “military facilities and infrastructure, including aircraft hangars, radar installations, runways, ammunition depots and other targets at King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait”, Saudi Arabia. It said the attacks were a response to a Saudi offensive, which involved more than 300 air strikes across Yemen over five days. There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia on the Houthi claims. On Sunday, the Saudi civil defence agency sent alerts for the city of Abha and the region around Khamis Mushait, but they were quickly lifted shortly afterwards. Fighting in Yemen’s more than 10-year civil war reignited in July, threatening a United Nations-brokered truce that halted large-scale violence in 2022, after the Houthis declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea. The fighting soon spilled over beyond the country’s borders, with the Houthis carrying out air attacks on southern Saudi Arabia, including oil facilities. Dozens of people were wounded in those attacks. Clashes in Yemen intensified last week after the Houthis captured parts of the country’s Red Sea coast, fortifying their hold on the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a key waterway which handles about 12 percent of global trade, including 11 percent of maritime oil and 8 percent of liquefied natural gas (LNG). The waterway has been an economic lifeline for Saudi Arabia and its oil exports, as the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively blocked by Iranian forces since the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran in February. The Houthis captured more strategic islands in the southern Red Sea, The Associated Press news agency reported on Monday, citing Yemeni government and Houthi officials. Houthi fighters were deployed on the islands of Greater Hanish and Lesser Hanish about 86 nautical miles (160km) north of the Bab al-Mandeb, according to two government officials and a Houthi official, the AP reported. Meanwhile, the International Organization for Migration said on Sunday the fighting in Yemen in recent weeks had displaced nearly 86,000 people. It added that some of those displaced by the conflict were fleeing Yemen altogether, with more than 2,000 people reaching neighbouring country Djibouti.

events.title: How Republicans secretly got Fetterman for their convention
events.summary: The biggest surprise of last week's Republican midterm convention began with an audacious request from the organizers to GOP Sen. Dave McCormick: Could he get Democratic Sen. John Fetterman, a fellow Pennsylvanian, to make an appearance? "I'll ask him," McCormick said. Within days, Fetterman — who's been increasingly at odds with the Democratic Party's liberal wing — was on board. Why it matters: Fetterman's 64-second video — calling himself a "common-sense Democrat," praising McCormick and vowing to work with President Trump to defend Pennsylvania's steel industry — represented Fetterman's biggest break yet with his party. Behind the scenes: According to three sources familiar with the talks, the idea for Fetterman to make the appearance emerged over the summer, as organizers of the Dallas convention sought what they called an "Oh sh*t" moment. They were looking to drive home a key midterm message — that Democrats are too extreme. Organizers discussed featuring "walk away" figures — people who had supported Democrats but had become disillusioned with the party. Republican operative Tony Sayegh, a leading convention organizer, was a driving force behind the idea, and Trump adviser Jason Miller backed the plan. Fetterman topped their list. Zoom in: Sayegh, a friend of McCormick's, took the idea to him in July. McCormick had developed a friendship with Fetterman as the Democrat grew more estranged from his party, particularly over many Democrats' criticism of Israel. Organizers knew getting Fetterman involved would be a massive coup. The intrigue: McCormick approached Fetterman carefully, knowing the backlash his Democratic colleague could face if he agreed to a role in the GOP convention. McCormick asked Fetterman to introduce him at the convention. A source said McCormick added: "I don't want you to do something that's not good for you." The two senators hashed it out over calls and texts for a few days. "I want to do it. I'm sure it will make people mad," Fetterman told McCormick, according to the source. "But you're my friend, and I want to introduce you." Fetterman's decision was driven by his friendship with McCormick, not a desire to help Republicans , said a source familiar with his thinking. Fetterman "had no interest in being a pawn in a larger Republican play," the source said. There was brief talk of Fetterman traveling to Dallas to introduce McCormick in person, but he decided against it. Instead, Fetterman proposed recording a video outside a steel mill near his home in Braddock, Pa. McCormick's team arranged for a videographer to meet him there. Fetterman didn't use a script. He riffed in front of the camera. He focused on introducing McCormick and highlighting their bipartisan work in support of Pennsylvania's steel industry. Neither McCormick nor convention organizers tried to alter what he said. The notion of Fetterman switching parties never came up, according to a source familiar with the deliberations. Organizers saw Fetterman's appearance as a jolt that would draw eyeballs to the first-of-its-kind midterm convention — and play big on social media. To preserve the surprise, organizers kept the circle tight. McCormick looped in his chief of staff, Mark Isakowitz, and only a few others. Miller was Sayegh's point of contact in the White House. Fetterman went even further: He told no one on his team, a source told Axios. The bottom line: Fetterman's appearance at Trump's convention deepened his estrangement from the Democratic Party. But Fetterman reiterated after his appearance that he isn't switching parties, calling himself a "lifelong Democrat" and saying that if Democrats win control of the Senate in November, he'd remain the "51st vote."

events.summary: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in The VAT’s The Problem campaign has called for hospitality VAT to be reduced from 20% to 10%. Your support helps us to tell the story From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. More than 800 hospitality businesses have written to the Prime Minister urging him to set out how he will introduce a lower rate of VAT . The VAT’s The problem campaign has called for the hospitality VAT rate to be reduced from 20% to 10%. Businesses involved in the campaign have signed a letter urging Andy Burnham to deliver on his public support in February for a lower rate of VAT for hospitality. The letter comes as Mr Burnham gathers business leaders in Downing Street on Monday to pledge to back entrepreneurs. The Prime Minister is expected to host a series of events in No 10 aimed at pitching his Government as a “partner for growth” that can offer a stable platform for investment in the UK. Reviving Britain’s high streets has been a key focus for Mr Burnham since he took over in No 10, promising to give councils new powers to block vape and betting shops and pledging to cut business rates for pubs. Notable names to sign the letter calling for a VAT cut include celebrity chefs Heston Blumenthal and Tom Kerridge and restaurants Bill’s, Franco Manca, Pizza Express, and Wagamama. Mr Kerridge said: “20% VAT is holding hospitality back”, adding that the sector “is different from many other businesses because so much of what we spend our money on is our teams”. Pubs, bars and brewers among the signatories include Fuller’s, Greene King, Robinsons Brewery, and Wetherspoon’s, as well as resorts such as Center Parcs, Haven, and Marriott International. UKHospitality said the “vast majority of the signatories are small and medium-sized businesses that operate venues at the heart of their communities”. In the letter, the signatories told Mr Burnham: “It’s time for a fairer tax burden for hospitality. Without action, closures will only continue to accelerate, jobs will continue to be lost and opportunities for young people reduced. “More than 370,000 people have signed the #VATsTheProblem petition calling for a 10% rate of VAT for hospitality, bringing the UK in line with the European average. “A lower rate of VAT for hospitality can turn closures into openings, lost jobs into new jobs, and boarded up high streets into thriving centres of community. “Alongside your policy to reform business rates for the high street, we urge you to bring forward your plans to deliver a lower rate of VAT for hospitality.” TV chef Mr Kerridge said: “It’s clear that the Prime Minister understands the importance of hospitality, and I was really encouraged to hear him make the case earlier this year for a lower rate of VAT for our sector. “The reality is that 20% VAT is holding hospitality back. “Hospitality is different from many other businesses because so much of what we spend our money on is our teams. “You can reclaim VAT on a product, but you can’t reclaim VAT on a person. “That makes a 20% rate particularly tough for a sector where labour is one of our biggest costs. “And this is all happening at a time when businesses are already dealing with rising wages, energy bills, food costs and business rates. “We’re seeing the consequences, with businesses closing their doors every single week. “That’s why hospitality businesses across the country have come together with one simple ask of the Prime Minister: deliver on your pledge and bring hospitality VAT down to 10%, in line with our European neighbours. “We don’t need another promise. We need action.” The campaign is supported by hospitality trade bodies and organisations, including UKHospitality, the British Beer and Pub Association, the British Institute of Innkeeping and Code Hospitality.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Passkeys promise fewer phishing headaches – and £600 a day off Whitehall's SMS bill MPs and peers tell UK to stop winging it on AI regulation 1 hour ago Revolut falls for fake government requests, hands over customer data 2 hours ago Britain's technology brief is now everyone's job and nobody's responsibility 3 days ago Whitehall's latest plan to get things done: Less Whitehall 6 days ago Britain reboots its space strategy with £7.8B already on the launchpad 6 days ago The UK government is giving more than 23 million people the chance to ditch passwords for passkeys – and could save itself a tidy sum on authentication texts in the process. Passkeys are being rolled out more widely across GOV.UK One Login following a trial involving more than 300,000 users, allowing people to sign in using a fingerprint, Face ID, or device PIN instead of entering a password and waiting for a two-factor authentication (2FA) code. The government says nearly one in ten daily One Login sign-ins are already being made using passkeys , which it claims are up to eight times faster than logging in with a username, password and 2FA code. There is also a less glamorous incentive for Whitehall: text messages cost money. The switch is already saving taxpayers nearly £600 a day in SMS costs, according to the government. Passkeys are designed to resist phishing. Rather than relying on a password that can be stolen, reused, or handed over to a convincing fake login page, a passkey uses cryptographic credentials tied to the website or app for which it was created. The biometric data or PIN used to unlock it remains on the user's device and isn't seen or stored by GOV.UK One Login. "Cyber criminals often look for the easiest route to access important accounts, which means login details remain a common target," said Jonathon Ellison, director for national resilience at the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC). "But passkeys offer a highly phishing-resistant alternative to passwords, frustrating attackers and saving the public time." The NCSC is encouraging users to switch, although passwords aren't disappearing just yet. Passkeys remain optional, and anyone who would rather continue signing in the old-fashioned way can do so. GOV.UK One Login is intended to provide a single account for accessing government services rather than requiring users to navigate a collection of separate sign-in systems. It is already used for services including checking State Pension details, managing tax services, and accessing childcare support. Digital Government Minister Stephanie Peacock said the rollout was intended to make government services both easier to access and harder for fraudsters to exploit. "Nobody enjoys hunting for a forgotten password or waiting for a text message code just to check their tax return or renew a document," she said. Whether Britain's 23 million One Login users share Whitehall's enthusiasm for replacing passwords is unclear. But with passkeys already accounting for almost 10 percent of daily logins – and every authentication text adding to the government's phone bill – there are at least a couple of reasons to keep nudging them in that direction.

events.title: Trump calls on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian diesel fuel, citing a global shortage
events.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump has called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian diesel fuel infrastructure, saying attacks are causing a global shortage KYIV, Ukraine -- U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage. He spoke after diesel prices in the U.S. hit a record on Friday , soaring past $6 a gallon on average. Ukraine has for months been targeting Russia’s oil and gas industry with long-range strikes, prompting fuel rationing across the country and causing Moscow to ban diesel exports in July, removing supplies from the already tight global market. But the global crunch also came after the war on Iran curtailed oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Fuel prices are weighing on Americans as they prepare to vote in midterm elections in November. Trump was asked by a reporter if he had spoken with Zelenskyy following his recent conversation with Russia’s Vladimir Putin. He responded by calling on Zelenskyy to halt strikes against Russia. “Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters on the sidelines of the Irish Open, which is being played at his Doonbeg golf club. “We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting, that’s hurting the world,” he said. According to a report published Friday by the International Energy Agency, net exports of diesel and gasoil from the Gulf countries in August stood at “just over a quarter” of what they were before the war on Iran began in February. “Disruptions to Russia’s refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses,” the IEA wrote. It added that in February, combined next exports of diesel and gasoil from the Gulf and Russia “accounted for almost 45% of global seaborne trade.” Kyiv says Russia's oil industry both funds and directly fuels Moscow's more than four-year-old invasion of Ukraine. Russia has ramped up its air campaign against Ukraine in recent weeks, using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce Ukraine’s defenses. Moscow’s attacks have targeted Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter in what officials say is meant to demoralize civilians. Civilians were killed and injured overnight into Sunday as Russia and Ukraine exchanged large-scale drone strikes. Two people were killed and 14 more wounded near an oil and industrial hub in Russia’s Tatarstan, according to local officials, while Ukrainian authorities reported on Russian drones pummeling the Black Sea port of Odesa and starting a fire near a border crossing with Poland. Millions dropped from SNAP food assistance as funding faces September uncertainty Irish leaders react after Trump says he'd 'love' to see a unified Ireland Man arrested in death of woman found hanging from tree in Mississippi The two Russian civilians died after a drone slammed into a tree near their parked car in the city of Nizhnekamsk, according to the office of regional head Rustam Minnikhanov. Nizhnekamsk houses a key cluster of oil refineries and other industrial plants. Mayor Radmir Belyaev said that a fire had broken out at an unspecified “enterprise.” Ukraine also claimed to have hit a major oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban, in Russia’s Krasnodar region near Crimea. The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) agency said its drones struck a key oil processing unit and the refinery’s tank farm overnight into Sunday. Krasnodar authorities said the strike on “an enterprise” in Slavyansk-on-Kuban injured three people and damaged an oil pipeline. Russian forces shot down 389 Ukrainian drones during the night, Russia’s defense ministry said Sunday. In Ukraine, at least nine people were injured in a “massive” Russian nighttime attack on Odesa, according to Serhii Lysak from the city's military administration. Odesa is home to Ukraine's main port hub on the Black Sea and has faced sustained drone and missile strikes, with Kyiv accusing Moscow of trying to choke off its exports. A Russian drone attack on Saturday struck a residential high-rise in Odesa , killing two people and injuring 26 others, Ukrainian officials said. Russian overnight strikes also pounded western Ukraine, though there were no immediate reports of casualties. One drone set fire to a gas station near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing with Poland, according to Ukraine's top diplomat and a spokesperson for the local customs force. “This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X. Ukraine’s border crossings with Poland are a conduit for much of the military and humanitarian aid sent by Western allies.

events.title: I'm in my 60s and can't find full-time work. I took Social Security early and filed for bankruptcy to stay afloat.
events.summary: Thomas Heep has struggled to land a full-time job for more than a year. Thomas Heep Thomas Heep was laid off last year and thinks age discrimination could be hindering his job search. He's working part time and collecting Social Security, but says he's just scraping by financially. Heep recently filed for bankruptcy and believes it was the right decision. This as-told-to essay is based on conversations with Thomas Heep, a job seeker in his 60s who lives in Denver. He was laid off in April 2025 and is still looking for full-time work. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I was laid off from my job as an operations manager on April 4, 2025. I've been looking for full-time work since then. I'm currently working part-time, delivering prescriptions to patients in the Denver area, and I started collecting Social Security in my 60s, before reaching my full retirement age of 67. Both combined aren't enough to pay all my bills. Earlier this year, I filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. I'm an only child and the last living member of my family. Not having a family to turn to definitely increases the pressure in a situation like mine. I recently had an in-person interview for a job that paid $20 an hour. I felt like the interview went well, and I'd be grateful to get the job. But there's always a part of you that thinks: I've worked all my life to maybe get to this. A $20-an-hour job. I feel like I'm basically starting at zero. The job search process feels broken My job search has been 99% online — LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor, and stuff like that. Looking for work primarily online wasn't new to me, as I'd landed my last job only about a year before I was laid off. But this job search has felt different. I think the system is broken. First of all, so many of the companies I apply to don't respond at all. I started working during a time when you could just walk into a business, maybe they had a "We're hiring" sign, and you could talk to somebody right there. That doesn't happen anymore. You have to go online and fill everything out, with a very high chance you'll never hear back. It's such a process now, and I don't think it's as effective as people think. Companies can also easily get buried by résumés when they post a job opening. A decent-paying job in a stable field will get hundreds of applications. "Work from home" roles are worse. I've seen application numbers in the 2,000s and higher. How is anybody going to get through that number of applicants? I also think companies are looking for people who fully match every skill they list and don't need any training. That's just not going to happen. Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . I believe my age is a major hurdle I believe age discrimination could be a big part of why my job search has been so challenging. Even if a company loves my résumé, skill set, and work history, they're going to look at my age and go: How long is he going to stay? He's close to retirement age. It's too risky. I've tried shortening my work history or omitting my age from my résumé, but I think they can still probably figure it out. Thomas Heep says his age may be making it harder to find full-time work. Thomas Heep At a recent in-person interview, they needed my driver's license, so they knew immediately how old I was. They asked whether I knew I would be on my feet all day and whether I could lift 50 pounds. It felt like they were trying to figure out whether I could really handle the work. For me, 50 pounds is nothing. If there's one thing that's gone right in my life, it's my health. But I struggled to figure out exactly how to convey that in an interview. I want to reassure them that I can do the work without coming across as egotistical. Regardless, I was proud that I'd gotten the interview in the first place. The company told me it had received over 200 applications for the job. I'm stuck between a rock and a hard place financially I'm scraping by financially. Since I started collecting Social Security before reaching my full retirement age of 67 , some of my benefits can be withheld if I earn above a certain amount. If I earn more than $24,480 from working this year, $1 in benefits is withheld for every $2 I earn above that amount. I'm stuck between a rock and a hard place. What else am I going to do? I have to have income somehow. I really don't have a choice. Earlier this year, I filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy after exhausting what I felt were my other options. So far, I think it was the right decision. My credit score actually went up after I filed, and bankruptcy ended up looking much better to me than some of the debt-consolidation programs I'd explored. With less income, I've had to learn how to budget. I used to think I was good at budgeting, but I really wasn't. I've become better at it because there's no soft landing here. I either work, or I'm screwed. This job search might be the greatest challenge of my life I've never been in this situation before. Has it affected me mentally? A hundred percent. I've gone through days where I don't want to get out of bed, and I have to convince myself to do this or that sometimes. It's especially hard when you look in the rearview mirror and look at what you've done in your career. I believe that every place I've worked at, I've made it better. To think that now, because of my age or whatever the case may be, that I can't get a job — it's devastating. But I just keep going. I keep grinding. You have to constantly convince yourself not to lose faith in a situation like mine. If you lose that, then you're going to be in trouble. Do you have a story to share? events.title: Researchers probe how Democrats could win working-class voters
events.summary: Democrats need to employ more populist rhetoric, run candidates perceived as non-elite, and steer away from progressive rhetoric like “abolish ICE” if they want to capture more working-class voters in future elections, according to new data shared first with Semafor. Researchers at the Center for Working-Class Politics talked to 40,000 adults from April to June to determine how Democrats can win more working-class voters without compromising other support. The strategy should also include leading with “working-class economics” and explicitly prioritizing members of the working class, the research found. Working-class voters moved away from Democrats if the candidates endorsed defunding police (by 5.7 points), letting transgender girls play girls sports (by 5.6 points), or gun control (4 points). These voters were interested in economic populism, but a candidate’s background couldn’t overwhelm cultural concerns: On those, said Jared Abbott, the center’s director, “it’s better for you to say something that actually connects with those voters and that you agree with than to say nothing.”

events.title: Cadbury cut two months off its supply chain lead time for a key chocolate-bar ingredient in one move
events.summary: Mondelez has opened a new $22 million chocolate ingredient facility in Malaysia. The investment brings a key part of the Cadbury maker’s chocolate supply chain closer to its Southeast Asian operations. The company sees further room for growth in snacking across Southeast Asia. American snack giant Mondelez International is cutting at least two months from its supply-chain lead time for a key ingredient used in Cadbury chocolate. The company opened a $22 million facility in Shah Alam, Malaysia, on Friday to produce chocolate crumb, an ingredient that contributes to the taste and texture of Cadbury's chocolate products, locally rather than importing it from Australia and South Africa. "Producing it directly in Shah Alam removes at least two months from our supply-chain lead time," Nitin Binnani, vice president of integrated supply chain for SEA at Mondelēz International, told CNBC. The new facility will reduce import and transportation costs as it looks to support volume growth across Southeast Asia in the coming years, he said. Shah Alam is Mondelez's sole Cadbury manufacturing hub for Southeast Asia, producing more than 130 varieties of chocolate and around 100 million bars annually, Binnani said. Cocoa prices have eased after a record-breaking rally over the past two years, which was fueled by adverse weather and poor harvests that drove up costs for chocolate makers, CNBC previously reported . Southeast Asia already plays a broader role in Mondelez's global manufacturing network, with individual sites serving both domestic and international markets, and the company sees further room for growth in snacking across the region, Binnani said. "Our Cikarang plant in Indonesia, for example, supplies products to nearly 40 countries including Australia and Japan, while Thailand operates as an export-oriented hub for gum and candy," Binnani said. Mondelez is also currently exporting crumb to Pakistan to help address supply disruptions caused by interrupted shipping channels, he said. Based in Chicago, Illinois, Mondelez owns snack brands including Oreo, Ritz, Cadbury and Sour Patch Kids. Mondelez is not the only U.S. company expanding chocolate-related production in Malaysia. U.S. agribusiness giant Cargill expanded its specialty fats production facility in Port Klang earlier this year , including capacity for ingredients used in chocolate manufacturing. Formerly known as Kraft Foods, the company was renamed Mondelez International in 2012 after spinning off its North American grocery business.
